{{Short description|Crystallographic concept}}
[[File:MillerIndices SydW.tif|thumb|The lattice planes created from the miller indices for (100), (010), (001), (110), (101), (011), (020), (002), (222), (111), (11̅1), with origin point showed by the yellow dot.]]
In [[crystallography]], a '''lattice plane''' of a given [[Bravais lattice]] is any plane containing at least three noncollinear Bravais lattice points. Equivalently, a lattice plane is a plane whose intersections with the lattice (or any crystalline structure of that lattice) are [[periodic functions|periodic]] (i.e. are described by 2D Bravais lattices).<ref name=Ash76>Neil W. Ashcroft and N. David Mermin, Solid State Physics (Harcourt: New York, 1976).</ref> A '''family of lattice planes''' is a collection of equally spaced parallel lattice planes that, taken together, intersect all lattice points. Every family of lattice planes can be described by a set of integer [[Miller indices]] that have no common divisors (i.e. are [[Coprime integers|relative prime]]). Conversely, every set of Miller indices without common divisors defines a family of lattice planes. In example figure 1 shows (100), (010), and (001) are a family of lattice planes and can be denoted by {100}. If, on the other hand, the Miller indices are not relative prime, the family of planes defined by them is not a family of lattice planes, because not every plane of the family then intersects lattice points.<ref>{{Cite book|last=H.|first=Simon, Steven|url=https://worldcat.org/oclc/1267459045|title=The Oxford Solid State Basics |date=2020|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-968077-1|oclc=1267459045}}</ref>

Conversely, planes that are ''not'' lattice planes have ''aperiodic'' intersections with the lattice called [[quasicrystal]]s; this is known as a "cut-and-project" construction of a quasicrystal (and is typically also generalized to higher dimensions).<ref>J. B. Suck, M. Schreiber, and P. Häussler, eds., ''Quasicrystals: An Introduction to Structure, Physical Properties, and Applications'' (Springer: Berlin, 2004).</ref>

[[File:MillerIndices CsCl.tif|thumb|The lattice planes for the miller indices (111), (100), (110), and (222) in CsCl cubic lattice. Where the pink atoms are Cs and the purple are Cl.]]

[[Miller indices]] is a notation system for lattice planes in crystallography. It is made from three integers h, k, and l. Written as (hkl). The values of these are given by the question g<sub>hkl</sub> = hb<sub>1</sub> + kb<sub>2</sub> + lb<sub>3</sub>. Where b is the basis of the reciprocal lattice for a given Bravais lattice. Each integer is related to the reciprocal lattice axis a, b, and c respectively. To find the plane indicated by the [[miller indices]], first take the integers (hkl) and dived 1 by them to get {{frac|1|h}},{{frac|1|k}},{{frac|1|l}} . Next take the Bravais lattice with the axis a,b,c and choose an origin. From the origin move on the axis by   respectively. For example, if the [[miller indices]] were (111) then you would get {{frac|1|1}},{{frac|1|1}},{{frac|1|1}} which equals 1,1,1 which means to move up each axis by 1 to find the plane from the origin. Figure 2<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Momma |first=Koichi |last2=Izumi |first2=Fujio |date=2011-10-29 |title=<i>VESTA 3</i>                     for three-dimensional visualization of crystal, volumetric and morphology data |url=https://doi.org/10.1107/s0021889811038970 |journal=Journal of Applied Crystallography |volume=44 |issue=6 |pages=1272–1276 |doi=10.1107/s0021889811038970 |issn=0021-8898}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |last=None Available |title=Materials Data on CsCl by Materials Project |date=2020 |url=https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/1199031/ |access-date=2026-05-22 |others=The Materials Project |publisher=LBNL Materials Project; Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL), Berkeley, CA (United States) |language=en |doi=10.17188/1199031}}</ref> shows the miler indices in a real crystal lattice: CsCl cubic crystal lattice (Pm3̅m space group).
